We analyze how VLA fine-tuning reorganizes instruction routing by comparing three architectures---OpenVLA (Llama-2-7B), TracVLA (Phi-3-mini), and NORA (Qwen2.5-VL-3B)---across four LIBERO task suites in trained and untrained conditions ($N = 2$ independent VLM-to-VLA transitions, plus one VLA-to-VLA transition).
Three findings emerge.
First, $R^2$ exit collapse---where action-relevant information encoded at intermediate layers is discarded at exit layers---is observed in all 6 VLM-to-VLA cells across two architectures; a chat-finetuned NLP control on the same backbone shows $\Delta R^2 \approx 0$, consistent with this effect being specific to action-oriented training.
Second, all trained VLAs exhibit moderate to large counterfactual sensitivity to instruction perturbation (Cohen's $d = 0.45$--$1.52$).
Third, early-layer instruction-dominant attention traces to base-model priors rather than VLA training.
These findings decompose VLA instruction routing into training-induced effects (exit collapse, counterfactual sensitivity) and inherited base-model priors (L1 attention), with consistency across two VLM-to-VLA transitions with distinct starting points.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Synthesis.}
VLA fine-tuning produces two training-induced representational changes---$R^2$ exit collapse and counterfactual sensitivity---that concentrate at the readout token (training shifts readout $R^2$ by $+0.069$ vs.\ image\_mean by $+0.015$).
L1 instruction attention is inherited from base-model pretraining (Phi-3-Vision: 32/32, Qwen2.5-VL: 13--14/16 before training).
VLA fine-tuning does not build instruction routing from scratch; it reorganizes downstream representations while preserving early-layer attention structure.

\paragraph{Cross-architecture consistency.}
Two independent VLM-to-VLA transitions converge on the same training-induced effects (observed in all 6 cells), compatible with task-structure constraints of causal-decoder VLA design.
OpenVLA provides supplementary VLA-to-VLA evidence, with exit collapse observed in 2/4 cells for spatially demanding tasks; however, the OXE pretraining confound limits direct comparison with VLM-to-VLA transitions.
Mid-layer probes outperform exit-layer probes for action prediction in architectures exhibiting exit collapse, suggesting potential efficiency gains from early-exit inference.
Correlating trained $\Delta R^2$ with LIBERO success rates yields a positive but non-significant trend ($\rho = 0.583$, $p = 0.10$, $n = 9$; Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Cross-architecture evidence rests on $N = 2$ independent VLM-to-VLA transitions; OpenVLA tests a different transition type.
All experiments use LIBERO; benchmarks with richer language grounding are needed.
We analyze only causal-decoder VLAs; flow-matching~\cite{black2024_pi0} and diffusion~\cite{ghosh2024_octo} architectures may differ.
NORA lacks 2 of 4 suite checkpoints, and each architecture is analyzed at a single trained checkpoint (extended discussion in Appendix~\ref{sec:extended_discussion_appendix}).

\paragraph{Conclusion.}
We analyzed three VLA architectures across four LIBERO task suites, comparing trained and untrained checkpoints.
Two training-induced effects---$R^2$ exit collapse (observed in all 6 VLM-to-VLA cells) and counterfactual sensitivity ($d = 0.45$--$1.52$)---differ consistently between trained and untrained conditions across architectures, while L1 instruction attention is inherited from base-model priors.
An NLP finetuning control ($\Delta R^2 = 0.000$) is consistent with exit collapse being specific to action-oriented training.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

\paragraph{$R^2$ action probes.}
Two-layer MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} ($d_\text{in} \to 256 \to 7$, ReLU) are trained to predict 7-D action vectors from frozen representations at each layer (Adam, lr${}=10^{-3}$, batch size 256, 50 epochs, early stopping patience 5).
Train/test splits follow demonstration boundaries (demos 0--39 vs.\ 40--49) to prevent within-trajectory leakage.
We report per-task macro-averaged $R^2$ with bootstrap paired comparisons (10{,}000 resamples).

\paragraph{L1 attention head profiling.}
At L1, each attention head is classified as instruction-dominant ($>50\%$ of readout-token attention allocated to instruction tokens) or image-dominant.
Results are reported as $k/N$ instruction-dominant heads, where $N$ is the total L1 head count: 32 for OpenVLA and TracVLA (MHA), 16 for NORA (GQA query heads).
Sensitivity analysis at thresholds from $30\%$ to $70\%$ confirms ordering robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:threshold_sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Counterfactual instruction perturbation.}
The instruction is replaced with four conditions: empty string, wrong task from the same suite, shuffled tokens, and paraphrased instruction.
A metric constraint arises from the trained/untrained asymmetry.
Trained models produce action outputs; their sensitivity is measured via Cohen's $d$ on action MSE (OpenVLA, TracVLA) or cosine distance on action representations (NORA).
Untrained VLMs (Phi-3-Vision, Qwen2.5-VL) do not generate actions; their sensitivity is measured via cosine distance on hidden representations, a metric with different scale and distributional properties.
Cross-metric ratios between Cohen's $d$ and cosine distance are therefore invalid (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).
OpenVLA's OXE-pretrained untrained checkpoint is the exception: because it produces actions, same-metric (Cohen's $d$) trained-vs-untrained comparison is possible for that condition.

\paragraph{$R^2$ action probes.}
To measure how much action-relevant information is linearly decodable at each layer, we train two-layer MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} to predict 7-D action vectors from frozen representations (architecture and training details in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}).
$R^2$ near 1.0 means the layer's representation nearly determines the action; a drop from peak to exit layer indicates that action-relevant information is discarded in later processing.
Train/test splits follow demonstration boundaries to prevent within-trajectory leakage.
Linear probes yield consistent patterns (Appendix~\ref{sec:linear_probe_appendix}), confirming that observed effects are not artifacts of MLP probe capacity.

\paragraph{L1 attention head profiling.}
To determine whether attention heads preferentially route instruction information to the readout position, each L1 head is classified as instruction-dominant ($>50\%$ of readout-token attention to instruction tokens) or image-dominant, reported as $k/N$ heads (32 for MHA, 16 for GQA).
Sensitivity analysis at thresholds from $30\%$ to $70\%$ confirms ordering robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:threshold_sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Counterfactual instruction perturbation.}
To test whether the model's actions actually depend on instruction content, the instruction is replaced with four conditions: empty string, wrong task, shuffled tokens, and paraphrased.
Trained models' sensitivity is measured via Cohen's $d$ on action MSE (OpenVLA, TracVLA) or cosine distance (NORA); untrained VLMs use cosine distance on hidden representations.
These metrics operate on different scales; cross-metric ratios are invalid (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).

We define $R^2$ exit collapse as $\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{peak}} - R^2_{\text{exit}}$, the drop in action-probe accuracy from peak layer to exit layer (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_matrix}).
All six VLM-to-VLA cells show clear collapse: TracVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} trained $\Delta R^2$ ranges from $0.138$ to $0.294$ (untrained: $0.009$--$0.048$), and NORA~\cite{hung2025nora} reaches $\Delta R^2 = 0.691$ on Goal, where exit-layer $R^2$ drops below zero (Figure~\ref{fig:r2_collapse}).
Under VLA-to-VLA conditions, OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla} shows task-dependent collapse: Spatial ($\Delta R^2 = 0.110$ trained vs.\ $0.052$ untrained) and Object ($0.121$ vs.\ $0.076$) exhibit clear collapse, while Goal ($0.016$ vs.\ $0.033$) and Long ($0.004$ vs.\ $0.016$) do not---consistent with collapse scaling with the representational distance between pretraining and target task.
A sign test across all six VLM-to-VLA cells confirms the direction ($p = 0.016$); across all ten cells, eight show trained $>$ untrained ($p = 0.055$).
A chat-finetuned control (Llama-2-7b-chat, same backbone as OpenVLA) shows $\Delta R^2 = 0.000$, confirming that exit collapse is specific to action-oriented training rather than a generic fine-tuning artifact.

We define $R^2$ exit collapse as $\Delta R^2 = R^2_{\text{peak}} - R^2_{\text{exit}}$, the drop in action-probe accuracy from peak layer to exit layer (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_matrix}).
Exit collapse is observed in all six VLM-to-VLA cells across two architectures: TracVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} trained $\Delta R^2$ ranges from $0.138$ to $0.294$ (untrained: $0.009$--$0.048$), and NORA~\cite{hung2025nora} reaches $\Delta R^2 = 0.691$ on Goal, where exit-layer $R^2$ drops below zero (Figure~\ref{fig:r2_collapse}).
Under supplementary VLA-to-VLA conditions, OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla} shows task-dependent collapse: Spatial ($\Delta R^2 = 0.110$ trained vs.\ $0.052$ untrained) and Object ($0.121$ vs.\ $0.076$) show collapse, while Goal ($0.016$ vs.\ $0.033$) and Long ($0.004$ vs.\ $0.016$) do not; the OXE pretraining confound limits direct comparison with VLM-to-VLA cells.

\paragraph{NLP finetuning control.}
To test whether exit collapse is specific to action-oriented training or a generic fine-tuning artifact, we probe Llama-2-7b-chat---the same Llama-2-7B backbone as OpenVLA, fine-tuned via SFT and RLHF for chat without an action head.
Across all 32 layers, $R^2 = 0.155 \pm 0.001$ with $\Delta R^2 = 0.000$, showing no peak-to-exit drop.
By comparison, OpenVLA (same backbone) exhibits $\Delta R^2 = 0.110$--$0.121$ on spatially demanding tasks.
This is consistent with exit collapse being specific to action-oriented training.

tool_args.old_string:
We analyze how VLA fine-tuning reorganizes instruction routing by comparing three architectures---OpenVLA (Llama-2-7B), TracVLA (Phi-3-mini), and NORA (Qwen2.5-VL-3B)---across four LIBERO task suites in trained and untrained conditions ($N = 2$ independent VLM-to-VLA transitions, plus one VLA-to-VLA transition).
Three findings emerge.
First, $R^2$ exit collapse---where action-relevant information encoded at intermediate layers is discarded at exit layers---is observed in all 6 VLM-to-VLA cells across two architectures; a chat-finetuned NLP control on the same backbone shows $\Delta R^2 \approx 0$, consistent with this effect being specific to action-oriented training.
Second, all trained VLAs exhibit moderate to large counterfactual sensitivity to instruction perturbation (Cohen's $d = 0.45$--$1.52$).
Third, early-layer instruction-dominant attention traces to base-model priors rather than VLA training.
These findings decompose VLA instruction routing into training-induced effects (exit collapse, counterfactual sensitivity) and inherited base-model priors (L1 attention), with consistency across two VLM-to-VLA transitions with distinct starting points.
